tours.name: The Five Falls
tours.blurb: Ten miles of cataracts that stopped every boat that ever tried — and made Lewis and Clark walk a month.

keys.cap: Black Eagle Falls, the uppermost of the five — named for the eagle Lewis found nesting on the island in June 1805.
Giant Springs — Clark measured it and called it the largest fountain he ever saw; two hundred million gallons a day, straight out of the Madison limestone.
The Great Fall itself, 87 feet — 'the grandest sight I ever beheld,' Lewis wrote, and then spent a month portaging around it.
The portage plain. Eighteen miles of cactus and hailstorms with cottonwood-wheeled wagons; the party staggered into the upper camp on July 2, 1805.

tours.name: Head of Navigation
tours.blurb: Two thousand three hundred miles from St. Louis, the steamboats tied up at one levee — the world's innermost port.

keys.cap: Fort Benton — fur post from 1846, then the head of steamboat navigation: everything Montana wore, drank, or dug with crossed this levee.

The Benton bottoms. In 1867 alone, thirty-nine steamboats made the passage; freight went out by ox train on the Mullan and Whoop-Up roads — the whiskey trade north to Blackfoot country is part of that ledger, and is said so plainly.
Loma, at the Marias mouth. When the Great Northern's rails reached Fort Benton in 1887, the levee's trade died in a season.
The 1890 sheet still engraves the ferry and the fort's old adobes — a port becoming a courthouse town.

tours.name: Decision Point
tours.blurb: In June 1805 the expedition camped nine days where two rivers met, betting the whole journey on which one was the Missouri.

keys.cap: Decision Point. The north fork ran muddy like the Missouri they knew; the south fork ran clear. Every man but the captains voted north — up what is now the Marias.
The Marias — Maria's River, for a cousin Lewis admired. The captains scouted both forks and chose the clear south fork, correctly, against the whole party's judgment.
Coal Banks Landing, where the low-water steamboats unloaded — and where the White Cliffs reach begins, 'seens of visionary inchantment,' as Lewis spelled it.
Into the Breaks. Beyond the sheet's corner the river runs wild to the Judith — the same white rimrock Bodmer painted in 1833.

tours.name: Into the Belts
tours.blurb: The river country's back yard: coal at Sand Coulee, silver at Neihart, and a railroad up Belt Creek to fetch both.

keys.cap: Sand Coulee and Stockett — the coal that fired the smelter stacks at Great Falls and the engines of the Montana Central.
Belt, in its coulee — Cascade County's first coal camp; Mortson's 1890 county map colours every working in the hills behind it.
Monarch, where the Belt Creek canyon narrows — the Montana Central climbed this grade in 1891 for the silver above.
Back to Great Falls — Paris Gibson's planned city at the falls, where water power, coal and ore met; the 1886 sheet was surveyed the year before the city boomed.
